Many small businesses keep records in an exercise book, on scraps of paper or in their heads. That works until you need an answer quickly: how much did I sell last month, which product makes the most money, who still owes me? The two spreadsheet programs you will meet most are **Microsoft Excel** and **Google Sheets**. They look and work in very similar ways, and almost every formula in this course is typed the same way in both. You can follow the whole course on either one, on a phone or on a computer.

A spreadsheet can only calculate what it understands. If you type **N5,000** or **5k**, it sees words, not a number, and your totals will quietly be wrong. This lesson teaches the habits that keep data clean, then how to make it readable with formatting.

The layout rules
**One row = one transaction.** Each sale, purchase or payment gets its own row.
**One column = one kind of detail.** Date in one column, item in another, amount in another. Never mix two details in one cell, such as 3 bags @ 2000.
**Headings in row 1 only**, short and clear, with the unit in brackets: Amount (₦), Weight (kg).
**No blank rows or columns** inside your records. Sorting, filtering and charts treat a blank row as the end of the data.
**Same spelling every time.** Transport and Transpot are two different categories to a spreadsheet. Later you will add drop-down lists to stop this.

Avoid merged cells and big decorative titles above your headings. A title such as MY SALES 2026 in row 1 with headings in row 3 confuses sorting, filtering, tables and charts. Put the title in the file name or the tab name instead, and keep row 1 for headings. If you want a heading to look wider, make the column wider rather than merging cells.

Spreadsheets follow the same order as school maths (BODMAS): brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. So =2+3*4 gives **14**, but =(2+3)*4 gives **20**. When in doubt, add brackets.

Put totals in the same place on every sheet, for example two rows under the last entry or in a separate summary area at the top. When you insert rows in the middle of a range, the SUM range grows automatically. Rows added after the last entry may not be included, so tap the total afterwards and check the range in the formula bar. Module 3 shows tables, which grow by themselves.

**On a computer:** select the cell with the formula, then drag the small square at its bottom-right corner (the fill handle) down. Double-clicking the square fills down as far as the data next to it goes.
**On a phone:** tap the formula cell, tap Copy, select the cells below (drag the blue handles), then tap Paste. This works in both apps.
Each copied formula adjusts its row automatically: =C2*D2 becomes =C3*D3 in the next row. Module 2 explains why, and when you must stop it.
Keeping your business file safe

**Save online.** Google Sheets saves to Google Drive as you type. In Excel, save the file to OneDrive and keep AutoSave on. A phone that is stolen or dropped in water should not take your records with it.
**Use version history.** Google Sheets: File, Version history. Excel with OneDrive: File, Info, Version History. You can go back to yesterday's copy if something is deleted.
**Download a backup** once a month (File, Download, Microsoft Excel .xlsx in Sheets; Save a Copy in Excel) and keep it somewhere else, such as email to yourself.
**Lock your phone** with a PIN or fingerprint. Your sheet may hold customer names, phone numbers and debts, which are personal data you must protect.
Spreadsheet scams

Do not open spreadsheet attachments from strangers, especially ones that ask you to 'Enable Content' or 'Enable Macros' to see an invoice or a payment alert. That is a common way of installing harmful software. Real bank alerts come by SMS or your banking app, not as spreadsheets.

In Module 1 you copied =C2*D2 down and it became =C3*D3, =C4*D4 and so on. That is a **relative reference**: the formula remembers the position of the cells relative to itself (two columns left, one column left), not their fixed addresses. Most of the time this is exactly what you want.

Sometimes, though, every row must use the **same** cell, for example one commission rate or one discount rate typed once at the top of the sheet. If you copy a normal formula, the address slides down with it and points at empty cells. The fix is an **absolute reference**, written with dollar signs: **$H$1**. The $ has nothing to do with money here; it means 'do not move'.

Worked example: Kemi's sales commission

For example, Kemi sells shoes in Lagos and pays her sales assistant 5% commission on every sale. She types the rate once in H1 as 5% and keeps sale amounts in column E, rows 2 to 5: 19000, 7500, 12000 and 4800.
Wrong way: in F2 she types =E2*H1 and copies it down. F3 becomes =E3*H2, but H2 is empty, so F3, F4 and F5 all show 0.
Right way: in F2 she types =E2*$H$1 and copies it down. F3 becomes =E3*$H$1, still pointing at the rate.
She adds totals: E7 =SUM(E2:E5) and F7 =SUM(F2:F5).
In January she raises the rate to 6% by changing only H1.
Commissions are ₦950, ₦375, ₦600 and ₦240. Total sales are ₦43,300 and total commission ₦2,165, which is exactly 5% of ₦43,300. At 6% every row recalculates at once and the total becomes ₦2,598.
Mixed references in a price grid

Mixed references lock only the row or only the column. They are handy for a quick price grid. Suppose unit prices sit down column A (A2 is 1200, A3 is 2500) and quantities run across row 1 (B1 is 1, C1 is 5, D1 is 10). In B2 type =$A2*B$1 and copy it across and down the whole grid. The column A part stays locked to the price, and the row 1 part stays locked to the quantity. C2 shows 6000 (1200 x 5) and D3 shows 25000 (2500 x 10), all from one formula.

Instead of $H$1 you can give the cell a name. Excel: select H1, type CommissionRate in the Name Box left of the formula bar and press Enter. Google Sheets: Data, Named ranges. Then =E2*CommissionRate works and reads like a sentence. Named cells behave like absolute references when copied.

The silent error: numbers stored as text

SUM adds numbers and quietly skips anything it sees as text. If one amount was typed as N5,000 or pasted from WhatsApp with a hidden space, it is left out and the total looks believable but is short. Signs to look for: the number sits on the left of the cell, Excel shows a small green triangle in the corner, or COUNT on the column gives a smaller answer than COUNTA.
Worked example: Chioma's total that was too low
For example, Chioma sells hair products in Port Harcourt. Her five sales on Friday were 12000, 18000, 5000, 9000 and 22000, but her sheet's SUM said 61000 while her calculator said 66000.
She types =COUNT(B2:B6) and gets 4, while =COUNTA(B2:B6) gives 5. One cell is text.
She scans the column: B4 shows N5,000 on the left side of the cell.
She retypes B4 as 5000 and applies her naira format.
In Excel she could also click the warning icon next to a green-triangle cell and choose Convert to Number.
COUNT now returns 5 and SUM returns ₦66,000, matching the calculator. Without the check she would have under-recorded Friday by ₦5,000.

**Cross-check totals.** Money in minus money out should equal the last running balance. Category totals should add up to the grand total. If two routes to the same number disagree, something is wrong.

The three functions
Pattern
Reads as
SUMIF

Add the amounts where the category matches

Writing conditions
Exact text: "Transport". Capital letters do not matter.
A cell holding the text: J2. This is how a summary table works, one category per row.
Numbers with signs go inside quotes: ">10000", "<=500", "<>0".
Joining a sign to a cell: ">="&K1 means greater than or equal to whatever is in K1.

Worked example: Bisi's expenses by category

For example, Bisi's October expenses sit in a tracker with Category in C2:C9 and Amount in G2:G9: Foodstuff 55000, Gas 9000, Packaging 7000, Transport 2500, Foodstuff 12000, Transport 1500, Packaging 3500, Transport 2000.
She lists categories in J2:J5: Foodstuff, Gas, Packaging, Transport.
In K2 she types =SUMIF($C$2:$C$9,J2,$G$2:$G$9) and copies it down to K5. The $ signs keep the ranges fixed while J2 moves to J3, J4, J5.
In L2 she types =COUNTIF($C$2:$C$9,J2) and copies it down to count entries per category.
K6 =SUM(K2:K5) gives the total. For trips she adds =AVERAGEIF(C2:C9,"Transport",G2:G9).
For large purchases she adds =COUNTIF(G2:G9,">5000").
Foodstuff ₦67,000 (2 entries), Gas ₦9,000 (1), Packaging ₦10,500 (2), Transport ₦6,000 (3), total ₦92,500, which matches =SUM(G2:G9). Average transport trip ₦2,000. Four expenses were above ₦5,000.
Always cross-check
The category totals must add up to the overall total of the Amount column. If they do not, a category is misspelt or missing from your summary list. This is the same cross-check idea from Lesson 2.3.
SUMIFS: more than one condition

**SUMIFS** adds rows that meet several conditions at once. Note the order is different: the range to add comes **first**. =SUMIFS(sum range, range1, condition1, range2, condition2, ...). For example, money spent on Transport in October only, with dates in column A:
=SUMIFS(G:G, C:C, "Transport", A:A, ">="&DATE(2026,10,1), A:A, "<"&DATE(2026,11,1))

DATE(2026,10,1) builds the date 1 October 2026 whatever your region setting, which avoids day-month confusion. Using 'less than 1 November' instead of 'up to 31 October' works for every month without worrying about 30 or 31 days. COUNTIFS works the same way for counting.
Best sellers and loyal customers

The same functions work on products and customers. On a Products summary, list each product and use =SUMIF(Tracker!D:D,A2,Tracker!E:E) to add up the units sold of the product named in A2 (with product names in column D and quantities in column E of the tracker). Sort the summary by that column to see your best sellers at the top. On the customer side, if you add customer names in column L, =COUNTIF(Tracker!L:L,"Mama Joy") counts how many times one customer bought from you. Customers with high counts are your loyal base; they are the people to tell first about new stock.
Whole columns and circular references

Ranges such as G:G (the whole column) are fine in both Excel and Google Sheets and save you from editing ranges later. Just never put the SUMIF formula itself inside the column it is adding, or you create a circular reference. Keeping summaries on a separate tab avoids this completely.
Customers and debts

Add a Paid column K (with a Paid or Unpaid drop-down) and a Customer column L to your tracker. Then =SUMIF(K:K,"Unpaid",G:G) gives the total owed to you and =COUNTIF(K:K,"Unpaid") the number of unpaid sales. =SUMIFS(G:G,L:L,"Mama Joy",K:K,"Unpaid") shows what one customer owes. A debtors list like this is often worth more than any chart.
Customer details are personal data

Names, phone numbers and what people owe are personal information. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 expects businesses to collect only what they need and keep it secure. Share summary totals, not customer lists, in groups; restrict who can open the file; and never post a debtors list publicly to shame customers.

On your sales log you can type just the product code and let the sheet fetch the price. That is what lookup functions do: find a value in one column and return the matching value from another column on the same row.

The lookup replaces flipping through a price list by hand.
XLOOKUP (newer, easier)

=XLOOKUP(what to find, where to look, what to return, [if not found]). On a Sales tab with the code in B2: **=XLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$A$100,Products!$D$2:$D$100,"Not found")**. If B2 is P03, it returns 3300. Then the amount is =C2*D2 as before: a quantity of 2 gives 6600.

XLOOKUP works in Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, Excel for the web and Google Sheets. It looks for an exact match by default, can return a column to the left or right, and the 'if not found' part replaces the #N/A error with your own message.
VLOOKUP (older, everywhere)

If your Excel is 2019 or older, use VLOOKUP. =VLOOKUP(what to find, table, column number, FALSE). For the same job: **=VLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$K$100,4,FALSE)**. The 4 means 'return the 4th column of the table', which is Selling price (A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, D is 4).
The code you search for must be in the **first column** of the table. VLOOKUP cannot look to the left.
Always finish with **FALSE** for an exact match. Leaving it out tells VLOOKUP to find an approximate match, which can quietly return the wrong product's price.
If you insert a new column inside the table, the column number may now point at the wrong column. XLOOKUP does not have this problem.
Lock the table with $ signs so it does not slide when you copy the formula down.
#N/A means not found

If a lookup shows #N/A, the code typed does not exist in your Products list, or has an extra space or a letter O instead of a zero. Check the code, or use a drop-down list of codes so only real ones can be chosen.

The routine in detail
**Daily (5 to 10 minutes):** enter the day's sales and expenses. Compare the transfer total with your Opay, Moniepoint or bank app and the cash total with the cash in hand.
**Weekly (15 minutes):** run the check cell, compare COUNT and COUNTA, look at the Reorder list, and chase any Unpaid sales.
**Monthly (30 to 45 minutes):** count stock, update the Products tab, produce the profit report, download a backup copy and start a new month.
**Quarterly:** look at three months of charts together and make one decision, such as dropping a slow product or changing a supplier.

First she types =E2*H1 and copies it down. The next row becomes E3 times H2. But H2 is empty, so every row after the first shows 0. This is the common mistake.
So she types =E2*$H$1 instead. Every copy still points at the rate. Her first sale of 19000 earns 950, and her total sales come to 43300 naira.
Total commission is 2165 naira. When she raises the rate to 6%, she changes only H1, and every row recalculates at once.
Build it
The sales and expense tracker
Type Sale and Expense the same way every time
Columns: Date, Type, Category, Details, Qty, Price
Amount: =E2*F2
Money in: =IF(B2="Sale",G2,0)
Money out: =IF(B2="Expense",G2,0)
Balance: J3 is =J2+H3-I3, copied down
Now build the tracker. Each row is one transaction: date, Sale or Expense, category, details, quantity and unit price.
The Amount column multiplies quantity by price.
Now the new function, IF. It makes a simple decision. The pattern is IF, a test, then what to show if true, then what to show if false.
So if column B says Sale, Money in shows the amount. If not, it shows 0. Text goes inside double quotes.
Money out works the same way, testing for Expense.
The running balance takes the balance from the row above, adds what came in, and subtracts what went out. Copy J3 down, not J2.
One warning. IF only works if the spelling matches exactly. Sales, or Sale with an extra space, will go to 0. In Module 3, a drop-down list removes this problem.

Loud errors and what they mean
Dividing by zero or by an empty cell. Fill the cell, or use IFERROR for expected gaps.
Maths on something that is not a number, like N2000. Retype it as a plain number.
The formula points to a cell you deleted. Undo straight away, or restore version history.
Every spreadsheet user makes mistakes. Loud errors show a code. Hash DIV slash 0 means you divided by zero or an empty cell.
Hash VALUE means maths on something that is not a number, like N2000.
Hash REF means the formula points to a cell you deleted. Press undo straight away.

Stock is often the biggest amount of money a small trader has tied up. An inventory sheet tells you what you have, what it is worth, and what to reorder before customers find empty shelves.

Products tab
Stock that tells you when to reorder
Closing stock = opening stock + stock in - units sold
Code, product, cost price, selling price
Opening stock, stock in, sold
Closing stock: =E2+F2-G2
Status: =IF(H2<=I2,"Reorder","OK")
Stock value at cost: =H2*C2
On a Products tab, give each product a short unique code, like P01, then its name, cost price and selling price.
Then type the opening stock, the stock you bought in, and the units sold.
Closing stock is opening stock, plus stock in, minus sold.
Set a reorder level for each product. If closing stock falls to that level, IF shows the word Reorder. Your sheet becomes an automatic shopping list.
Stock value is closing stock times cost price.
For example, Funke has 6 detergents left, and her reorder level is 8, so it says Reorder. Her stock on hand is worth 80250 naira at cost.
Lookups
Fetch the price from a code
XLOOKUP
Newer Excel and Google Sheets
Exact match by default
Can say Not found
VLOOKUP
Works in older Excel too
Code in the first column
Always end with FALSE

On your Sales tab, type just the product code, and let a lookup fetch the price. XLOOKUP finds the code in the Code column and returns the selling price from the same row. If the code is P03, it returns 3300.
If your Excel is 2019 or older, use VLOOKUP. The code must be in the first column of the table.
And always finish with FALSE. Leaving it out can quietly return the wrong product's price. If you see hash N A, the code was not found. Check for a letter O typed instead of a zero.
Key words
Sales: money earned from selling
Cost of goods sold: what the sold goods cost
Gross profit: sales minus cost of goods
Net profit: gross profit minus running costs
Margin: profit divided by sales
Now profit. Sales is the money earned from selling. Cost of goods sold is what the goods you actually sold cost you: opening stock value, plus purchases, minus closing stock value.
Why not sales minus purchases? Because if you stock up heavily, the month looks like a loss even though the goods are still on your shelves.
Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods. Net profit takes away running costs too, like rent, transport, data and power.
A margin divides profit by sales, so you can compare months of different sizes.
